title: It's a jug
hook: if you love a jug, say "I love a jug," and if it breaks you won't be thrown (Enchiridion 3)
carry: clay breaks; that's part of what clay is

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was desire: for a beginner, set it down for now and choose lightly. Your line was gently, for now.

A mug that nobody else is allowed to use. Chipped, maybe. A gift, maybe. Somebody's grandmother's. One morning it slips off the counter, and the small crack on the tile floor can land like bad news. Everyone in the kitchen knows it's a mug. And still. Epictetus, teaching in a Greek town, picked almost exactly this object to start with: not a great loss, a clay pot from the kitchen. Today: it's a jug.
screen: `THE MUG NOBODY ELSE USES.` → `A CRACK ON THE TILE.` → `IT'S A JUG.`

segments.voice: In section three of the handbook, Epictetus says: with everything that delights you, or is useful, or that you love, remind yourself what kind of thing it is. Start with the smallest things. If you're fond of a jug, say: I'm fond of a jug. Then when it breaks, you won't be thrown. The point isn't to love it less. You can still drink from the good mug every morning; the practice is to name it truly while you have it. Clay breaks; that's part of what clay is. Said ahead of time, the breaking is a sad thing that happened, not a betrayal. Then the hard part. The same section doesn't stop at jugs. When you kiss your child or your wife, Epictetus goes on, say to yourself that you are kissing a human being, and then if one of them dies, you won't be overwhelmed. Readers argue about this line. Some find it cold, a way of guarding the heart against the people it should be open to. Others hear it as tender: everyone you love is mortal, and saying so can make each goodbye at the door count. The text itself doesn't settle it, and you don't have to either. Why start small? Epictetus is a trainer, and nobody lifts the heaviest weight on the first day. Practice on the jug, the phone screen, the favorite sweater, and learn the move where it costs little.
screen: `SAY WHAT KIND OF THING IT IS.` · `LOVE IT, AND NAME IT TRULY.` · `THE HARD LINE: A HUMAN BEING.` · `BEGIN WITH THE SMALLEST THINGS.` · then, large: `IT'S A JUG.`

segments.voice: Choose one small thing you're fond of, a cup, a pen, a pair of shoes, a plant, and hold it or rest your eyes on it. Name it plainly, without coldness, the way you'd say it's raining: this is a cup, and cups break. Then notice what's left: you still like it, maybe a little more.
Epictetus, whose small practice names what you love for what it is, starting with the smallest things, so its breaking doesn't throw you. Today's word.
Your line: clay breaks; that's part of what clay is. Love the thing, and know what kind of thing it is. Day three hundred thirty-five, done.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism name a cherished object plainly to themselves, 'this is a cup, and cups break', practicing on small things first.
